The tambourin de Béarn is a chordophone, a rectangular box zither sounded by striking with beaters the strings stretched over a wooden resonator. The player hangs the instrument on the arm or shoulder, plays a three-hole one-handed pipe (the galoubet) with one hand and strikes the strings with a cloth-wrapped stick in the other; the pipe and the string drum are usually used as a pair, like a pipe and tabor. It is found in France and the Pyrenees, and in Zuberoa it provides the musical background for traditional dances and for the annual carnival show, the maskarada.

演奏時將長方形木製音箱掛在手臂或肩上，一手持單手笛，另一手持覆亞麻布的槌敲擊琴弦: To play, the rectangular wooden soundbox is hung on the arm or shoulder; one hand holds the one-handed pipe and the other strikes the strings with a linen-wrapped beater. The sound comes from the whole set of strings struck at once by the beater, the strings tuned in octaves vibrating together to give a sustained effect, which can be light or heavy. The first thing for a beginner is to hold the instrument steadily and to judge the angle of the stroke so that all three courses sound together; because there is no plucking string by string, it is relatively easy to start on.
蒙塔古指出，Tambourine de Bearn在中世紀已見於圖像並持續使用，: Montagu notes that the tambourine de Bearn appears in images from the Middle Ages and has been in continuous use, under the older names chronon or chorus. It appears around the fifteenth century and took root in the Pyrenees, becoming a common instrument of the western Pyrenees, usually paired with a three-hole pipe to accompany traditional dances and the annual maskarada carnival of the villages of Soule. In the twentieth century it declined in Bigorre, Béarn and Soule, and after the Second World War it almost stopped outside the Ossau valley; at the same time it was played, under names such as salterio, with a pipe on a small scale in the highlands of Aragon. From the 1970s it has come back to life.

貝亞恩手鼓為弦鳴樂器，發聲來自箱形齊特琴上縱向張弦，以包布琴槌整體敲擊。來源未載: The tambourine de Bearn is a chordophone, sounded by striking as a whole with a cloth-wrapped beater the strings stretched lengthwise over a box zither. The source gives no clear range, only three to eight strings, commonly six in three courses, mostly tuned in octaves to the tonic of the three-hole pipe, with five or six strings sometimes tuned in fifths. A stroke sounds two notes at once, like a chorus, and a sustained chord can be kept up. The volume runs from very soft to strong, controlled by the force of the stroke. Unlike a psalterium, which is strummed or plucked, it strikes the strings with beaters; and unlike a drumhead it sounds by the vibration of strings.
